summary.text: Quantum cryptography uses quantum properties such as entanglement, measurement disturbance and superposition to carry out encryption tasks.
Data encoded in a quantum state cannot be copied perfectly, and reading it changes it, so eavesdropping on a quantum link can be detected.
Its best-known use, quantum key distribution, lets two parties share a key without a third party learning anything, with security that can be proven mathematically.

facts.label: Early idea
facts.value: Wiesner's conjugate coding, from the early 1970s, published in 1983

facts.label: Ekert's protocol
facts.value: Proposed in 1991, using Bell's inequalities for secure keys

facts.label: Classical limit
facts.value: Classical encryption cannot be guaranteed beyond about 30 years

facts.label: QKD protection
facts.value: Can protect electronic records for up to 100 years

facts.label: Who sells it
facts.value: Firms include ID Quantique, Toshiba and QuintessenceLabs

items.prompt: Eve taps the line while Alice and Bob build a shared key. What gives her away?

options.label: The key becomes shorter each time
Her tapping makes the line louder
Discrepancies appear that Alice and Bob notice
The message is deleted from the network

items.explain: If Eve tries to learn about the key, discrepancies arise and Alice and Bob notice.

items.prompt: A hospital must keep patient records secret for many decades. Why could quantum key distribution suit it better than classical encryption?

options.label: It protects records for up to 100 years, versus about 30 for classical
It compresses records so they fit on much smaller hospital drives
It lets doctors skip the login step for patients who visit often
It makes records readable by every hospital in the world at once

items.explain: Scientists cannot guarantee classical encryption beyond about 30 years, while QKD can protect records for up to 100.

items.prompt: Alice and Bob have just established a key with quantum communication. What do they typically do next?

options.label: Destroy it and start over with a fresh one for each word
Use it for classical encrypted messages, such as a one-time pad
Send all of their future messages as single photons only
Publish it openly so that everyone can double check it

items.explain: Once established, the key is usually used for classical encrypted communication, for instance symmetric cryptography like a one-time pad.

items.prompt: Quantum key distribution is called unconditionally secure, but it still needs one safeguard. Which?

options.label: Alice and Bob must meet in person each day
Eve must be limited to a small computer
The parties must be able to authenticate each other
The channel must be completely free of noise

items.explain: Minimal assumptions remain: quantum mechanics holds and Alice and Bob can authenticate each other, otherwise a man-in-the-middle attack is possible.

items.prompt: A secure key must cross a long, noisy fibre. What can keep the link secure over that distance?

options.label: A thicker cable with much more shielding around the fibre
Quantum repeaters that purify segments before joining them
Sending the same key several times in a row to be safe
Switching over to a purely classical channel for the trip

items.explain: Quantum repeaters purify segments of the channel before connecting them, allowing secure communication over a noisy channel.

items.prompt: Wiesner's early scheme put two messages into one photon's linear and circular polarization. What could a receiver do with it?

options.label: Decode either message, but not both
Decode both messages together at once
Decode neither without a second photon
Copy it and decode both of them later

items.explain: With conjugate observables such as the two polarizations, either property may be received and decoded, but not both.
